catalog_quote: Accent. Gogodala has phonemic stress, as is shown by umína wind, úmina buttress. In bi-syllabic words the stress falls generally on the first syllable, in tri-syllabic words on the second syllable. Sequences of /i/, /u/, and a more open vowel can be regarded as diphthongs (/ei, ɛi, ai, eu, ɛu, au, ou, ua/) or triphthongs (/uai, iou/). [Voorhoeve 1970: 1265] ... There are no tones, and stress is phonemic, as shown by ùmina buttress versus umìna wind. [Voorhoeve 1975: 354]

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (25 pp., ANU scan with scanned layer). extracted text of pdf p. 20 (printed p. 1265) gives, under the heading "Accent" in "B. A SKETCH OF GOGODALA PHONOLOGY": "Gogodala has phonemic stress, as is shown by um?na wind, umina buttress. In bi-syllabic words the stress falls generally on the first syllable, in tri-syllabic words on the second syllable. Sequences of /i/, /u/, and a more open vowel can be regarded as diphthongs (/ei, Ei, ai, eu, EU, au, ou, ua/) or triphthongs (/uai, iou/)." The scanned drops the accents; the page image we hold shows them clearly: umína 'wind' (stress on the second syllable) and úmina 'buttress' (stress on the first). The other reader's quote is verbatim. C…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is contrastive (minimal pair umína 'wind' vs úmina 'buttress'), but the default position is the first syllable of two-syllable words and the second syllable of three-syllable words, i.e. the penultimate syllable in the word lengths the author reports; no rule is given for longer words. The language has no tones.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress is said to be phonemic, so lexical exceptions exist (umína 'wind' with second-syllable stress); the positional rule is hedged with 'generally'. Sequences of /i, u/ plus a more open vowel are treated as diphthongs/triphthongs (one syllable), which bears on syllable counting.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress in isolated lexical items from a wordlist, grammatical notes and a few short texts collected by Voorhoeve during a short visit to Balimo in 1966 (his note 3); citation forms, not connected speech. Language of the Balimo area (central Gogodala).
new_statements.identity_note: Voorhoeve's data are from Balimo (central Gogodala area, 1966 visit); Riley's 1930 wordlists suggest dialect diversity of which nothing is known (Voorhoeve 1970 n. 3). Waruna [wrv] is possibly a dialect of Gogodala (Voorhoeve 1975: 335) but no stress data for it. No separate glottocode issue; the statement is about gogo1265 proper.

sources.note: Appendix B 'A sketch of Gogodala phonology', subsection 'Accent', p. 1265 (pdf p. 20): stress is phonemic (umína 'wind' vs úmina 'buttress'); bisyllables generally stressed on the first syllable, trisyllables on the second. sources.note: Bibliography only. Descriptive refs: Neuendorf n.d. (grammar sketch), Neuendorf 1977 (study of one feature). Other refs are ethnographic (Lyons 1926, Haddon 1916, Wirz 1934, Crawford 1981, Weymouth 1978/79, Hays 1991), wordlists (Ray 1907, 1914, 1923; Riley & Ray 1930-31), overviews (Capell 1969, Voorhoeve 1968/1970/1975, Reesink 1976, Lean 1986), Bible portions.
Source listed: Neuendorf no date, 'Gogodala grammar'; coder Jay Latarche; no stress/tone feature values displayed.
Phoneme tables only (p t k b d g m n s l w j; i u e o ɛ a with allophones); nothing on stress. References Capell 1969, Voorhoeve 1970, Voorhoeve 1975.
